extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent prosecutors and patent practitioners (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the USPTO subject-matter eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106) on patent claims, including Step 1 (statutory categories) and the two-part Alice/Mayo test (Step 2A/2B) with Pathways A/B/C and streamlining advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: The Four Categories of Statutory Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole falls within one of the four statutory categories in 35 U.S.C. 101: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and controlling case law are provided: a process (method) requires action or steps; machines are concrete things consisting of parts or device combinations; manufactures are tangible articles given new form, quality, property, or combination by man-made means; compositions of matter are combinations of two or more substances (including composite articles). For non-process categories, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. It is not necessary to identify a single correct category so long as the claim falls into at least one. Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to any statutory category include products without physical form (e.g., data per se, software per se) and transitory signals. See cited Federal Circuit and Supreme Court cases for illustrations (e.g., Digitech, Nuijten, Microsoft v. AT&T, Chakrabarty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and exclude claims covering non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 1 after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that could be a carrier wave), the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1 (Step 1: NO). Examiners should point out the BRI, recommend an amendment where possible to narrow to statutory embodiments, and, if appropriate, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 using form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01). If amendment could place the claim within a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three eligibility pathways (A, B, C) and when to use each
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the flowchart to determine eligibility via Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident), Pathway B (Step 1 YES and Step 2A NO), or Pathway C (Step 1 YES, Step 2A YES, Step 2B YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pathway A: claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible via a streamlined analysis (see MPEP §2106.06). Pathway B: claims that fall in a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A NO) are eligible without Step 2B. Pathway C: claims that fall in a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A YES), but recite additional elements (individually or in combination) that amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B YES) are eligible. If uncertain whether a streamlined analysis is appropriate, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If not eligible at any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A (Alice/Mayo Part 1): Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, mathematical formulas, scientific principles, mental processes, and similar concepts. There are no bright lines between exceptions; many concepts can fall under multiple labels. The concern underlying these exceptions is preemption, but preemption is not a standalone test — the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) resolves preemption questions. Evaluate Step 2A after construing claims under BRI and reviewing disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry: Prong One — Recitation of a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recitation can be explicit ('set forth', e.g., mathematical equation in Diehr or laws in Mayo) or implicit/descriptive (e.g., concept of intermediated settlement in Alice). Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception (require further analysis) from claims that merely 'involve' an exception (which may be eligible). Example: a claim stating 'operates in accordance with F=ma' recites a law of nature; a teeter-totter claim that does not state the physical law merely involves it and is not directed to an exception. See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b)/(c) for detailed analyses of abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural phenomena, and products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry: Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If additional elements do not integrate the exception, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B to determine whether it amounts to significantly more (an inventive concept). Mere recitation of the exception is insufficient; additional elements that are themselves judicial exceptions (or merely add another abstract idea) do not integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims that recite multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions, apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions, and avoid unnecessarily parsing the claim into multiple exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea in different limitations), for efficiency the examiner may select one exception and conduct the analysis for that exception; if the claim is shown to integrate or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, consider it eligible. If multiple abstract ideas or multiple laws of nature are recited together, do not parse them but consider them together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B when possible. Examples and case law are provided (Bilski, Mayo, Alice, Univ. of Utah v. Ambry Genetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere inclusion of an exception does not equate to being directed to it
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a judicial exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) under Prong One may nevertheless not be 'directed to' that exception under Prong Two if the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prong Two distinguishes claims that simply recite an exception from those directed to that exception. If there are no additional elements in the claim beyond the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, the claim cannot be eligible. Examiners should recommend amendments where possible to resolve eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and non-limiting illustrations of non-statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to products without physical or tangible form do not fall within statutory categories and are therefore non-statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples include: information/data per se, computer program per se (software claimed as a product without structural recitations), transitory signal transmissions (signals per se), and paradigms/business models. The guidance cites Digitech (intangible device profile), Microsoft v. AT&T (software without medium), In re Ferguson (business model), and Nuijten/Mentor Graphics (transitory signals). Where a product lacks physical embodiment, it does not meet the statutory category requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs and best practices when making 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is clearly not within the statutory categories (Step 1 NO), the examiner must reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and use specified form paragraphs; if the claim could be amended to become statutory, recommend amendment and continue analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting for lack of statutory subject matter, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 (see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but the disclosure suggests an amendable path to statutory subject matter, document that and proceed to determine whether an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C. It is a best practice to recommend amendments and explain the BRI that leads to the rejection.
